source.title: The Illusion of Cross-Lingual Safety in Low-Resource Languages
source.authors: Abigail Oppong; P SAM SAHIL; Tadesse Destaw Belay; Maryam Ibrahim Mukhtar; Esmael Abdu; Tassallah Abdullahi; Jessica Oparebea; Saminu Mohammad Aliyu; Idris Abdulmumin; A. Chilala; N. Ladislaus; Alfred Malengo Kondoro; Lemofouet Valdini Douglace; Shamsuddeen Hassan Muhammad; S. Yimam

record.tranche_reason: Extends geometric analysis of refusal-direction transfer to four low-resource African languages and several model checkpoints. It measures cross-lingual representations but does not causally intervene on the direction.
record.gate_note: The study measures English and target-language difference-in-means directions, their alignment, and downstream refusal proxies. It does not ablate or add a direction, edit weights, or test jailbreak suppression or robustness. Values used only for layer selection and results cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study computes the Arditi-style difference-in-means refusal direction in English and in four low-resource African languages, using three instruct models. It reports how well the directions align at layer 16 (cosine, signed retained component). This bears directly on whether the direction carries across languages (V6). It is geometric and correlational only: no ablation, addition or weight edit, so V1–V5, V7 and V8 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that target-language harmful prompts, literal or culturally localized, are weakly connected to English safety geometry: under 10% of the English refusal signal is retained in most pairs. Llama-Swahili is a localized partial exception. Effects are architecture- and prompt-form-dependent. They call multilingual safety alignment 'superficial' and present their evidence as correlational, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-safe mean activation directions and geometric alignment measures, but focuses on cross-lingual transfer and does not perform the original causal ablation or addition interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by language, architecture, and literal versus culturally localized prompt form; layer-wise drift is also reported as non-uniform across depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Average probability of emitting a standard refusal sequence is about 1.05–1.15% across target-language harmful prompts. It varies by model (Llama about 2%, Qwen about 0.3%) and by language (Hausa about 3.6–4%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruct models rarely refuse harmful prompts in low-resource African languages (a behavioural refusal rate, separate from direction geometry).

fits_no_version.finding: Literal and culturally localized target-language harmful-minus-safe directions are nearly identical (cosine 0.95–0.996) but still diverge in projection onto the English direction across layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-language refusal-related directions are stable across prompt form while staying orthogonal to the English direction.

record.problems: No causal interventions; the authors note the observational framework, restriction to 7B–8B models, lack of a safety-aligned moderately resourced control language, and possible distortion from low-resource-language tokenization. They also caution that the behavioral refusal proxy can be depressed by generation instability. Several appendix findings are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: To remain within the 60-row limit, omitted the separate Table 2 dot-product and mean-drift metrics, language-level and model-level Table 4 breakdowns, and qualitative PCA/probe findings. The retained-component and English-versus-target cosine rows capture the primary cross-lingual direction-alignment results; omitted measures are in Table 2, Figures 3–8, and Table 4.

untested.parts: Causal transfer: ablating or adding the English direction for target-language prompts. Transfer across model variants or from base to instruct. Larger models. Safety-aligned languages. Layers other than 16 (shown only in figures for dot product and probes).
Ablation, addition, and capability retention: none performed.
Multi-direction structure within a language is not analysed.
Harm judgment versus refusal decision is not separated.
The effect of training method or timing is not tested. AfriqueQwen is used only for PCA visuals.

missing.what: Literal vs cultural cosine within each language (0.95–0.996)
Per-model and per-language refusal probabilities and SLL
Zero-shot transfer of the English linear probe across layers, including elevated Swahili confidence in Llama and Mistral

record.verdict_notes: Partial requires cosine ≥0.10 or about ≥5% retained; values below this, which the authors call near zero, were set to absent. Small negative cosines (to -0.15) were kept as absent, not reversed, because they indicate near-orthogonality rather than an opposite refusal effect. The reader's 'supports' label for Llama-Swahili was downgraded to limits_scope: a cosine of 0.46 and 27% retained is partial, and the authors call it a partial exception. All results come from a single layer (16). The languages are not safety-aligned in these models, unlike the safety-aligned languages of the cited Wang et al. (2025), so the results narrow rather than directly contradict the claim of universality across safety-aligned languages.

versions.untested_parts: Causal mediation, projection-out ablation, adding the direction, and effects on general capability.
Weight-edit removal of refusal in released models.
Whether attacks suppress the direction or training against its ablation adds robustness.

Whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or composed of a dominant direction plus additional directions. Language-specific cross-language alignment is not a test of these alternatives within a language.
Whether harmfulness judgment is separately encoded from the refusal decision.

Transfer beyond the four studied languages and tested checkpoints; causal transfer of the direction. The study also does not establish that the geometric measurements are equivalent to successful behavioral refusal.
How refusal training method or timing determines whether a removable direction exists.
Reasoning models that reason before answering.

relation.reason: Its own Table 2 results bear directly on whether the English refusal direction is shared with target-language harmful-minus-safe directions.

tranche.reason: New setting (four low-resource African languages, three 7-8B instruct models) with diff-in-means directions compared by cosine and retained component at layer 16. There is no causal ablation, so it is not T1.

source_check.notes: The study is observational: one layer (16), 7-8B models, no ablation or addition, and no safety-aligned control language (stated in its limitations). Target-language safe prompts come from other corpora (Aya, GhanaNLP) than the harmful DNA translations, so the target directions may partly reflect dataset differences. Twi gets split across verdicts (Mistral counted absent, Llama/Qwen partial), though the authors describe Twi overall as 'modest positive alignment'.

statements.correction: Group cosine -0.1489 (Mistral SWA ctx) to 0.0762 (Mistral TWI lit); retained -7.7326% to 3.6790%. Llama-SWA cos 0.4626/0.4577, retained 27.31%/27.73%. Llama/Qwen Twi cos 0.1019-0.1430, retained 4.94-8.57%. Observational, layer 16 only, no ablation or addition.
statements.problem: For the challenged group the top of the cosine range is 0.0762 (Mistral-Twi literal), not 0.07. This study only measures geometry, so the clause that low-resource directions 'do not transfer' cannot come from it.

statements.problem: Says English vs Amharic/Hausa/Swahili directions are near-orthogonal in Llama and Qwen. Llama-Swahili is not: cosine 0.4626, about 27% retained.

statements.correction: Near-orthogonal except Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Swahili (cos 0.4626, 27.31% retained). Twi in Llama and Qwen is modestly aligned (cos 0.10-0.14). All at layer 16, observational.
statements.problem: Calls Amharic/Hausa/Swahili directions near-orthogonal to English without excluding Llama-Swahili (cosine 0.46).
The visible part does not name this study. Counting it among the V6 challenges/limits_scope studies fits its verdicts. It adds no causal evidence.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: This is the study's localized transfer exception: cosine alignment is 0.4626 and 0.4577, with retained components 27.3063% and 27.7349% (R13, R14, R37, R38).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Positive but weakly aligned language-model pairs at layer 16
reader_labels.reason: Some target-language directions have positive alignment, but reported retained components are generally small and the paper describes transfer as uneven (R1, R2, R7, R8, R15, R16, R18, R19, R23, R24, R31, R32, R39, R40, R43, R47, R48).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Negative or near-zero English–target alignment across the reported model-language pairs
reader_labels.reason: Many measured directions are negatively aligned or near zero, and the paper concludes that transfer is not reliable across the studied language-model pairs (R3-R6, R9-R12, R17, R20-R22, R27-R30, R33-R36, R41-R46).
